items.title: Food and Medicine Homology Focus in 2026
items.summary: This perspective paper examines the anticipated direction of the food and medicine homology field as it transitions from traditional empirical knowledge toward contemporary scientific approaches. The authors outline a framework built around scientific rigor, mechanistic understanding, precision medicine, and modernized industrial processes. Research priorities identified include identifying active components, elucidating multisystem interaction mechanisms involving gut microbiota, and investigating emerging biological phenomena such as phase separation and immunometabolic reprogramming. Applications are expected to advance toward dynamic, personalized health management for challenges such as chronic disease and aging, supported by multidimensional personal data and artificial intelligence. The field is also projected to evolve industrially through synthetic biology, intelligent delivery systems, and sustainable manufacturing practices.
items.citation: Mengyao Li, Gui-Fen Wu, Feng Lu et al.. Food and Medicine Homology Focus in 2026. Food & medicine homology.. 2026

items.title: Characterization of a prototype parallel-plate $^{238}$U fission chamber with DD and DT fusion neutron sources
items.summary: This paper describes the experimental validation of a uranium-based fission chamber detector system designed to monitor neutron emission across an extremely wide dynamic range during high-performance fusion plasma operations in the SPARC tokamak. The detector uses a parallel-plate geometry combined with borated polyethylene collimation to preferentially detect unscattered fusion neutrons from both deuterium-deuterium and deuterium-tritium reactions. Testing with both types of neutron generators confirmed that the detector efficiency matched vendor specifications and that the device responded linearly across the relevant measurement range, with results agreeing well with neutronics simulations. Additional characterization demonstrated that the detector maintains reliable performance under tokamak-relevant environmental conditions, including exposure to stray magnetic fields and signal degradation challenges associated with long cable runs. The authors conclude that this fission chamber design, when combined with appropriate neutron shielding and pulse height discrimination, provides a robust solution for fusion power measurements in the planned neutron diagnostics system.
items.citation: V. Hagenlocker, R. A. Tinguely, X. Wang et al.. Characterization of a prototype parallel-plate $^{238}$U fission chamber with DD and DT fusion neutron sources. arXiv. 2026

items.title: SkillProx: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Proximal Textual Gradient Descent
items.summary: This paper investigates how large language model agents can improve their performance on recurring tasks by refining procedural knowledge stored as reusable textual artifacts called skills. The authors identify two key limitations in existing skill-refinement frameworks: the absence of explicit feedback linking diagnoses to outcomes, and the treatment of skill deletion as a generic editing operation rather than a principled consolidation mechanism. To address these gaps, they propose SkillProx, a framework inspired by proximal gradient descent that combines a forward stage performing closed-loop, regression-aware diagnostic editing with a backward stage that decomposes skills into auditable knowledge units and applies utility-based consolidation, demotion, or removal. Evaluated across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks using multiple backbone language models, SkillProx outperforms the strongest gradient-based baseline in average accuracy. Ablation studies confirm that the closed-loop diagnosis and proximal refinement components each contribute independently to the observed gains.
items.citation: Mingxuan Zheng, Yujin Zhou, Chuxue Cao et al.. SkillProx: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Proximal Textual Gradient Descent. arXiv. 2026

items.title: A quantum geometric mechanism for chiral domain wall metastability: Application to twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides
items.summary: This paper investigates how band topology and quantum geometry influence magnetic domain wall behavior in ferromagnets with time-reversal conjugate Chern bands. The authors show theoretically that smooth magnetic textures in such systems can generate a dipole density transverse to a domain wall, controlled by a dimensionless geometric coefficient related to the second Chern form of the occupied band projector in mixed momentum and order-parameter space. This dipole response, though not quantized, enables domain walls to become metastable at finite radius through competition between dipolar repulsion and surface tension, even under finite Zeeman fields. Applying this framework to a realistic model of twisted molybdenum ditelluride, the authors find that the geometric coefficient changes sharply at a transition between topologically distinct ferromagnetic phases within the valley-polarized state, explaining recent pump-probe experiments in which long-lived excitations persist far beyond the saturation field but abruptly vanish at an intermediate displacement field. The work establishes metastable chiral domain walls as sensitive probes of band quantum geometry and identifies them as an intrinsic bottleneck for ultrafast optical manipulation of moiré ferromagnets.
items.citation: Nisarg Chadha, Qiang Gao, Eslam Khalaf et al.. A quantum geometric mechanism for chiral domain wall metastability: Application to twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides. arXiv. 2026

items.title: ResidencyRL: Reinforcement Learning in Simulated Clinical Environments
items.summary: This paper investigated whether reinforcement learning in simulated clinical environments could improve the sequential decision-making capabilities of large language model-based clinical AI agents, drawing an analogy to medical residency training. The researchers developed ResidencyRL, a framework that trains an AI agent through extended multi-turn simulated patient encounters using LLM-based patient simulators capable of adversarial behavior, with rewards structured around diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety. The trained agent showed meaningful improvements in diagnostic accuracy under adversarial conditions and substantially reduced rates of missed clinical red flags compared to the base model, with the improvement attributed in part to reduced premature diagnostic closure. Blinded expert clinicians strongly preferred the trained agent in direct comparisons, and the agent demonstrated generalizable gains across multiple held-out clinical benchmarks spanning different evaluation frameworks. The authors conclude that complex clinical reasoning can be effectively cultivated through multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulation, while noting that prospective validation in real-world clinical workflows is still required before clinical utility can be established.
items.citation: Valentin Liévin, Samuel Schmidgall, Tim Strother et al.. ResidencyRL: Reinforcement Learning in Simulated Clinical Environments. arXiv. 2026

items.title: LSEAD: A Privacy-Preserving LLM-Based Speech Analysis Framework for Early Alzheimer's Disease Screening
items.summary: This paper investigated the use of large language models for early Alzheimer's disease detection through speech analysis, motivated by the need for non-invasive, cost-effective, and privacy-conscious screening tools. The proposed framework, LSEAD, automatically transcribes speech recordings, extracts text embeddings using locally deployed open-source large language models, and applies dimensionality reduction via principal component analysis before classification, ensuring that no patient data is shared externally. The system was evaluated on two established benchmark datasets for Alzheimer's-related speech analysis. Results indicate that the large language model-derived embeddings generalize well across datasets and improve classification accuracy over existing methods, with gains particularly evident for early-stage detection. The authors conclude that their framework offers a practical, secure, and scalable approach to early Alzheimer's disease screening in real-world clinical settings.
items.citation: Xin Wang, Yingchao Huang, Yuhan Su et al.. LSEAD: A Privacy-Preserving LLM-Based Speech Analysis Framework for Early Alzheimer's Disease Screening. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Depth-Wise Probing and Pruning of the Planning Token in a Driving Vision-Language-Action Model
items.summary: This paper investigates how depth within a large language model backbone contributes to action planning in a vision-language-action model for autonomous driving, where a single planning token carries the entire plan. The researchers decoded this planning token at every layer of a deep decoder and measured both how well navigation commands could be linearly predicted from the token's representation and how compatible the token was with the model's native trajectory planner. They found that high-level semantic intent becomes linearly decodable very early in the network, while trajectory-level compatibility with the deployed planner improves gradually across all layers, suggesting that planning information is present early but not yet in the format the planner expects. By ranking layers according to the angular perturbation they introduce to the planning token, the authors identified and pruned the least impactful layers, achieving a meaningful decoder speedup with only a modest increase in open-loop trajectory error. The study concludes that significant depth redundancy exists in this architecture for driving planning, though the authors note findings are specific to the evaluated model checkpoint and benchmark setup.
items.citation: Harisankar Babu, Benjamin Coors, Christopher Lang et al.. Depth-Wise Probing and Pruning of the Planning Token in a Driving Vision-Language-Action Model. arXiv. 2026

items.title: The piezochiral effect
items.summary: The paper introduces a previously unrecognized physical phenomenon called the piezochiral effect, in which mechanical strain induces and controls chirality in solid-state materials. Through symmetry analysis, the authors show that uniaxial strain can generate chirality in a broad class of achiral crystals that contain structural fragments of opposite handedness within each unit cell, with the induced handedness tunable by changing the direction of strain or by switching between compressive and tensile strain. This theoretical framework was experimentally validated using optical activity measurements on a crystal under applied strain, confirming that strain can serve as a conjugate field that couples linearly to chiral structural order. The discovery addresses a longstanding challenge in materials science—the absence of a universal field for rational chirality control—and provides a continuous, bidirectional mechanism for switching handedness in solids. The authors suggest broad implications for applications spanning spintronics, asymmetric catalysis, and enantioselective biological interactions.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it introduces a previously unrecognized physical phenomenon—the piezochiral effect—whereby mechanical strain can be used to control chirality, expanding the known family of strain-responsive material properties. Its potential applications span a broad range of advanced fields, from photonics and spintronics to biosensing and quantum information.
items.citation: Z. Zeng, M. Först, M. Fechner et al.. The piezochiral effect. Nature. 2026

items.title: Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP
items.summary: The paper investigated how mitochondrial metabolism contributes to the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), an inflammatory programme driven by senescent cells that promotes tissue dysfunction. The researchers found that an upregulated mitochondrial pyruvate–citrate–acetyl-CoA axis in senescent cells increases acetyl-CoA availability, which supports histone acetylation at SASP gene loci and is required for robust transcription of those genes, working alongside mitochondrial DNA-driven activation of inflammatory transcription factors. Inhibiting SLC25A1, the mitochondrial citrate exporter, reduced histone acetylation at SASP loci and dampened the inflammatory programme in cell-based experiments. In aged mice, SLC25A1 inhibition decreased chromatin accessibility at SASP loci, reduced inflammation, and improved healthspan. Together, these findings describe a mitochondrial metabolic checkpoint that epigenetically enables innate immune signalling output in senescent cells, identifying a mechanism through which SASP can be selectively controlled.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals a mechanistic link between mitochondrial metabolism and the epigenetic activation of inflammatory genes in senescent cells. The finding that blocking a specific mitochondrial transporter can dampen this process highlights a potential therapeutic strategy for slowing age-related decline.
items.citation: Hélène Martini, Jodie Birch, Francisco Madeira Marques et al.. Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP. Nature. 2026

items.title: Avalanche-like intercalation and intraparticle correlations in graphite
items.summary: This paper investigated the lithium intercalation dynamics in graphite, the dominant negative electrode material in lithium-ion batteries, focusing on the poorly understood dilute staging regime where symmetry-breaking phase transitions occur. Using operando optical microscopy, the researchers directly observed that graphite particles undergo rapid, localized deintercalation–intercalation events in which micrometre-sized regions transform within seconds, rather than progressing smoothly. These events resemble "avalanches" seen in disordered materials, characterized by abrupt jumps between multiple metastable states. A modified random field Ising model was developed to link these avalanche dynamics to static structural disorder within the graphite, successfully reproducing both the apparently continuous stage transitions and the observed avalanche statistics. Spatio-temporal analysis of sequential avalanche events further revealed heterogeneous connectivity across particles, underscoring the critical role of local disorder in governing phase-transition behavior in layered battery materials.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it directly visualizes avalanche-like lithium intercalation and deintercalation events in real time, revealing how local disorder controls phase-transition dynamics and ion transport in battery electrodes—insights that could inform the design of more efficient lithium-ion batteries.
items.citation: Jiho Han, George Phillips, Alice J. Merryweather et al.. Avalanche-like intercalation and intraparticle correlations in graphite. Nature. 2026

items.title: Weight-four parity checks in a spin-shuttling architecture
items.summary: This paper investigates silicon spin-qubit devices as a platform for quantum error correction, focusing on a sparse array architecture where coherent spin shuttling provides long-range qubit connectivity. The researchers built a device featuring a shuttling bus with four interaction sites called bus stops, enabling dynamic qubit transport and interaction without relying on charge sensing across most of the device. Using shuttling and quantum non-demolition measurements, they achieved universal control over an effective five-qubit processor and configured the connectivity needed to implement surface-code stabilizer plaquettes supporting both X- and Z-type parity checks up to weight four. The parity checks were used to generate multi-qubit entanglement across all qubit combinations in the array, including a five-qubit Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state representing one of the largest genuinely entangled states demonstrated with gate-defined semiconductor spins. The work establishes modular calibration and operational protocols for sparse spin-qubit arrays and argues for the near-term feasibility of quantum error-correction experiments using mobile spin qubits.
items.why_notable: This work draws attention because it demonstrates that incorporating a shuttling bus into a silicon spin-qubit device enables parity checks up to weight four, a key milestone for quantum error correction, while showcasing the broader feasibility of shuttling-based architectures in semiconductor quantum processors.
items.citation: Brennan Undseth, Nicola Meggiato, Yi-Hsien Wu et al.. Weight-four parity checks in a spin-shuttling architecture. Nature. 2026

items.title: Enzymatic glycosylation and amidation reshapes polyene bioactivity
items.summary: This paper investigated the biosynthetic pathways of polyene natural products, a class of antifungal compounds whose clinical utility is hampered by severe toxicity and poor aqueous solubility. The researchers discovered and characterized previously undescribed polyene biosynthetic pathways, identifying unusual glycosyltransferase enzymes capable of attaching sugars to polyene scaffolds and demonstrating that an amidotransferase enzyme could be repurposed to convert the problematic carboxylate group of polyenes into alternative chemical functionalities. By combining the introduction of a second sugar with carboxylate modifications, the team generated new polyene variants with enhanced antifungal potency and reduced toxicity. Crucially, these improved compounds are accessible through fermentation or enzymatic synthesis rather than the costly and inefficient total chemical synthesis routes previously required. The findings suggest that enzymatic tailoring of polyene scaffolds offers a cleaner and more practical route to next-generation antifungal therapeutics.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it uncovers new biosynthetic pathways and unusual enzymes that modify polyene scaffolds with additional sugars, yielding previously undescribed compounds with improved potential as safe and effective antifungal treatments producible through clean, efficient fermentation.

items.title: A digitally controlled silicon quantum processing unit
items.summary: This paper introduces a quantum processing unit built from silicon exchange-only qubits, designed with commercial scalability in mind. The system integrates a custom cryogenic CMOS controller, a high-density superconducting ribbon cable, and a low-noise qubit device featuring an array of exchange-coupled quantum dots configurable to host up to eighteen exchange-only qubits. By combining these components, the researchers demonstrated single-qubit and entangling gate performance that improves on the previous exchange-only state of the art by an order of magnitude. To validate the system, they implemented both a distance-five repetition code and a distance-two quantum error-detecting code, comparing experimental results against simulations. The work argues that this integrated approach, leveraging compatibility with advanced semiconductor manufacturing and simplified control signals, provides a viable pathway toward utility-scale quantum computing with manageable hardware and operational requirements.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it demonstrates a silicon quantum processing unit capable of high-fidelity multiqubit circuits in which all control signals are generated by an integrated cryogenic digital controller — a significant step toward scalable, fully integrated quantum hardware. The combination of digitally programmable cryogenic control electronics with a low-noise qubit device connected via a high-density superconducting cable addresses key engineering challenges in scaling up silicon-based quantum systems.
authors: Members of the HRL Quantum Team and Collaborators
items.citation: Members of the HRL Quantum Team and Collaborators, Michaël Abraham, Edwin Acuna et al.. A digitally controlled silicon quantum processing unit. Nature. 2026

items.title: A global view of human centromere variation and evolution
items.summary: This paper investigated the sequence diversity, population variation, and evolutionary dynamics of human centromeres, regions essential for chromosome segregation that have been difficult to study due to their highly repetitive nature. The researchers assembled thousands of complete human centromeres from a large, diverse cohort spanning multiple continental and population groups, and developed new bioinformatic tools specifically designed for centromeric sequence analysis. They discovered extensive previously unknown variation, including novel centromere haplotypes, new alpha-satellite higher-order repeat variants, mobile element insertions in a substantial fraction of centromeres, and a notable prevalence of di- and tri-kinetochore configurations. Comparative analysis revealed dramatic variation in mutation rates across chromosomes, evidence of archaic hominin introgression shaping some centromeres, and a finding that the kinetochore site itself is the most rapidly mutating region within the centromere. Based on these findings, the authors propose a model of an evolutionary arms race between centromeric sequence and the proteins that bind it, driving rapid and ongoing evolution of these genomic regions.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it provides the first comprehensive, fully sequenced view of centromere diversity across a large, globally diverse human cohort, uncovering structural features and unusually high mutation rates that illuminate how these essential chromosomal regions evolve.
items.citation: Shenghan Gao, Keisuke K. Oshima, Shu-Cheng Chuang et al.. A global view of human centromere variation and evolution. Nature. 2026

items.title: In situ structure of the poxvirus portal complex
items.summary: This paper investigated the structure of the portal complex in poxviruses, which are large double-stranded DNA viruses responsible for diseases including smallpox and mpox. Using cryo-electron tomography combined with subtomogram averaging and computational structure prediction, the researchers determined the molecular architecture and protein composition of this pore-like structure that spans the poxvirus core wall in vaccinia virus. They found that the portal complex is a hexameric assembly comprising three conserved poxviral proteins arranged in distinct layers, with one protein forming the central chamber, a second hexamer decorating the exterior, and a third binding as a hexamer of dimers on the interior side. Additionally, the viral helicase required for genome release was shown to associate with the portal complex by docking onto its exterior rim during infection, providing mechanistic insight into how the virus releases its genetic material and messenger RNA into host cells. The authors propose that this structurally defined portal complex represents a promising target for the development of antiviral therapeutics against poxviruses.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals the atomic-level architecture of a previously uncharacterized portal complex in vaccinia virus, captured in its native context using cryo-electron tomography. The findings illuminate how this conserved hexameric structure physically connects to core viral processes—including genome packaging, messenger RNA release, and uncoating—offering fundamental new insight into poxvirus biology.

items.title: In situ structures of plant photosystem supercomplexes
items.summary: This study investigated the native structural organization of plant photosystems within intact chloroplast membranes, which had previously been unknown despite the availability of structures from isolated, purified components. Using in situ cryo-electron microscopy, the researchers directly imaged rice chloroplasts and determined the structures of photosystem supercomplexes in their natural membrane environment. They resolved a large PSII–LHCII supercomplex containing additional antenna trimers not seen in purified preparations, and excitation energy transfer calculations based on this native architecture closely matched in vivo measurements, supporting its physiological relevance. They also identified multiple asymmetric PSII–LHCII dimer configurations and higher-order assemblies, leading to the proposal that PSII forms a structural skeleton that shapes thylakoid membrane morphology and drives grana stacking. High-resolution structures of PSI-containing supercomplexes were additionally obtained, collectively providing the first molecular framework for understanding how native photosystem architecture achieves the remarkable efficiency of photosynthetic light-to-electron conversion.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it captures the plant photosystem supercomplex structure directly within its native membrane, preserving proteins and lipids that are typically lost during conventional purification—offering an unprecedentedly complete view of the intact photosynthetic architecture.
items.citation: Jiao Li, Eduard Elias, Kai Zhang et al.. In situ structures of plant photosystem supercomplexes. Nature. 2026

items.title: Over 20,000 precolonial earthworks in the Southwest Amazonia
items.summary: Using canopy-penetrating LiDAR technology flown over thousands of kilometers of flight in southwestern Amazonia, researchers investigated the true geographical extent and quantity of precolonial geometric earthworks that had previously been detectable only in deforested areas. The study combined existing earthwork data with new LiDAR documentation to overcome the longstanding limitation that forest cover concealed most of these structures from conventional detection methods. The findings reveal that the cultural area studied alone contains as many earthworks as had previously been estimated for all of Amazonia combined, suggesting the scale of monument-building civilization there was vastly underestimated. The researchers further propose that the total human population of this region during an early period of the first millennium was in the range of several million people. They conclude that if comparable results emerge from other parts of Amazonia, prevailing estimates of precolonial population density and its lasting influence on Amazonian soils, forest structure, biodiversity, and global climate models will need substantial revision.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because LiDAR technology has revealed a dramatically higher number of precolonial earthworks than previously thought, with one region alone containing as many such structures as had been estimated for the entire Amazon basin. The findings substantially revise the understood scale of ancient human landscape modification in Amazonia.

items.title: Miniaturizing and modifying natural proteins with Raygun
items.summary: Raygun is a generative artificial intelligence framework designed to miniaturize, modify, and augment natural proteins in ways that mimic the large-scale coordinated sequence changes seen in natural protein evolution. The core conceptual innovation is encoding each protein as a probability distribution in a fixed-dimensional space derived from protein language model embeddings, rather than as a variable-length sequence, making proteins of any length directly comparable and manipulable. Controlled by just two parameters governing substitutions and length changes, the framework can shrink or expand proteins while preserving predicted structural integrity and functional sites. In experimental validation, the approach successfully miniaturized fluorescent proteins and TurboID, a synthetic biotin ligase used in proteomics, and generated epidermal growth factor variants with enhanced receptor-binding affinity compared to the wild type. These results demonstrate that protein function can be faithfully captured in a length-agnostic representation, enabling computational access to the kinds of evolutionary sequence transformations that have previously been beyond the reach of protein design methods.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it introduces an AI-driven approach that can shrink and redesign natural proteins while preserving their original structure and function, opening new possibilities for engineering biological molecules.
items.citation: Kapil Devkota, Daichi Shonai, Yiwei Mao et al.. Miniaturizing and modifying natural proteins with Raygun. Nature. 2026

items.title: The past and future impact of climate change on childhood malaria in Africa
items.summary: This study investigated whether human-caused climate change has altered the burden of childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa, addressing a longstanding scientific debate about climate change and disease. The researchers analyzed the relationships between temperature, extreme precipitation, and malaria prevalence, and modeled both historical impacts and future projections under varying greenhouse gas emission scenarios. They found that while rising temperatures have likely increased malaria in East and southern Africa, this has been offset by a reduction in cases in West Africa, resulting in a negligible net continental impact to date. Looking ahead, climate change is projected to marginally accelerate malaria elimination in the highest-burden regions of West and central Africa, though high-elevation areas of East and southern Africa face meaningful increases in cases under higher warming scenarios. The study concludes that limiting future warming could prevent a notable number of excess malaria cases in vulnerable regions by the end of the century, while providing a methodological framework for quantifying the true global health burden of climate change.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it uses climate and econometric modelling to show that human-induced climate change is already reshaping where and how severely childhood malaria burdens fall across Africa, with implications for how that burden may shift in the future.
